So I think that if you're engaged in the business, and, you know, there's a reference to interstate or foreign commerce, so I'm thinking they're casting a pretty wide net, and you deliver videos, it seems most naturally read -- and some of you are maybe suggesting I'm most -- not most naturally reading "consumer," but I actually think I'm most naturally reading all 15 words. But I think, most naturally read, this would capture Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, all of these things, because they're certainly in business and they are delivering videos. Now, like, I don't want to put two feet on that because I could be back in some court arguing no, no, no, that, you know, it means something slightly different. But I think it's tough given that Congress clearly wanted to capture the -- the -- the -- the department stores and the grocery stores. And that's why I really think the most natural way to narrow this statute is to get the definition of "consumer" right and limit it to the consumers -- and, again, we're -- we're talking about the (a)(4) definition. But the (a)(4) definition's kind of baked right in to the definition of "consumer." And that's why I think it would have been redundant if -- I mean, you know, just to make the redundancy point one more time, I mean, (a)(4) is already baked in and already says a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material. So I suppose what Congress could have said in the definition of "consumer" is consumer means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials from a video tape service provider, which, of course, is a provider of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Right, right. Yeah.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: But that would be hopelessly awkward and redundant. And it -- it just underscores that if Congress had done both, it would have been redundant, and I think there was a perfectly good reason it left "goods or services" unmodified.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, the statute means what the statute means regardless of the -- of the consequences, but it would be interesting to know whether "in the business of" means deriving any sort of commercial advantage from providing access to videos on a website because that would seem to impose huge retroactive liability on a broad, broad range of entities. And I'm not sure I understood Mr. Hammack's definition of what it means to be "in the business of." Maybe he'll take another shot at that on -- on rebuttal.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: Yeah. I -- I must confess I did not understand it either. And I don't think it explains away Chick-fil-A. And just to put it in concrete terms, if you look at the complaint in this case, he alleges that there are over a hundred thousand subscribers to 247Sports.com that he wants to represent in a class action. Now I'm not great at math, but $2500 per plaintiff in a class action that includes at least a hundred thousand people, I think, is $250 million of liability in this case alone. And then you look at the Chamber brief and all those footnotes, you look at The Retail Litigation Center appendix and all of those cases, and there's a reason, I think, as you alluded to, that every district court judge that looks at this thinks this cannot be right, this is crazy. And I would suggest that a careful textual reading of all 15 words in this definition actually gets you to the result that, yes, it's not right.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: All right. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, some very intelligent circuit court judges have disagreed with you. The linchpin of your argument is that the transaction that some -- that makes someone a VPPA consumer must be the same one that generates PII. But the VPPA refutes that. "(D) governs the use of personally identifiable information" -- I'm quoting -- "obtained in any manner as evidence in some governmental proceeding." So you don't have to be a consumer in there. And it requires destroying such information as soon as practicable. Those provisions apply regardless of whether the information concerns a consumer. So, if the statute explicitly envisions that PII can exist without a consumer, I don't understand why it's absurd that a consumer might exist who hasn't yet generated but will generate PII because you're only liable if you are disclosing PII of someone's video-viewing. So what's -- I don't understand.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: So I do think there is a fundamental difference between having PII without a consumer and having a consumer that has no PII. Now, as we point out in our brief --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, no, a consumer will have PII because you're going to disclose PII. You're only liable --

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: No, no --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: -- whether -- what you're saying that it's different than if the consumer doesn't create it at that moment of the transaction.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: No, what I'm saying is, actually, under his view as I understand it, if you go into the Blockbuster, the last one, the brick-and-mortar store, you buy your dog bandana, and then you never look at the Blockbuster website, then you are a consumer in his view, but you have no PII. You are an inchoate VPPA consumer. And I think that is far more anomalous than --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. Then why? When you finally buy something, it is what you buy, that video-viewing, that's being protected.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: Well, you don't have to buy anything. And that's another anomaly. See, under the statute Congress wrote, if you walked in to a -- even a video store and they gave you a video, you're not protected by the statute. You have to have a video transaction. And what makes his position and I would -- I would respectfully suggest consumers without PII so anomalous is they essentially make this free online viewing of videos that otherwise doesn't make anybody a consumer and then they retroactively become a consumer because they bought a chicken sandwich 10 years later, they look -- they subscribed to the local newspaper, they signed up for a free email. I don't think that makes any sense. And I do think it does damage to the statute that having the converse doesn't because, as I've alluded to, all of the consent provisions are premised on the idea that the person that can provide consent is the consumer.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I just want to make sure I understand your view of (a)(3). So this is the PII includes information which identifies a person as having requested or obtained specific video materials. What does "includes" mean, do you believe?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: So I think that it means something different from "means." I think it does set a floor. And that's why I don't think the definition of PII can do the limiting --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, what kind of floor are you saying? In other words, does it include information which identifies a person as having requested or obtained other materials or services? I mean, your bandanas or your La-Z-Boys, do you think that there's no requirement that the person have requested or obtained video materials or services?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: Well, it's tricky, right, because, if we're going to be literal, I mean, "includes" --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, I want to -- I want to know what you -- you think.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: So --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Does it include bandanas and La-Z-Boys?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: So I would say that it doesn't. But it's hard to get there from a literal reading of the text because the textual definition is just an "includes" definition. Now I know from the Senate report, which I read, that Congress didn't want to protect private information about dog bandanas or furniture that you bought from a department store. So, if we're going to be faithful to the intent that was reflected in the Senate report, we have to figure some way to limit this statute so that it protects video information and not bandana information. And I would respectfully suggest that, you know, you could do it, and I -- I would suppose I might even argue for it someday, but it's hard to get the limit from a definition that's an inclusive definition. And I think the better place to get the limiting principle is from the definition of "consumer."

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Gorsuch?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Do you disagree with the American Newspaper amicus brief that "similar" would at least require content like full-length movies and television shows that were on video tape lining Blockbuster shelves?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: Ultimately, when that issue comes up, I would -- you know, in that --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: You're going to -- you're going to take that position?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: I am going to take that position.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: You'd agree with newspapers that that -- that that -- that -- that is a distinction?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: And I might even go one further and agree with Judge Randolph that they have to be --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Physical?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: -- physical.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: Because, you know, materials is kind of physical.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. Thank you.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: So, if you -- yeah.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Do you concede that Salazar has standing?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: We haven't argued that he doesn't. And I guess this is what -- if I could -- I think the best answer to that is I think it depends on what you make of page 11 of the Meta brief. I don't know if you have it in front of you, but it's -- you know, it's got this gobbledegook. And that's -- that's what's disclosed to a third party. And so I take it the question would be, is the disclosure of gobbledegook to a third party sufficiently close to the common law analogue of disclosing personal information to a third party to satisfy Article III? That's a tricky question. I mean, if you want us to, we can brief it. I would really hate for the Court to reject -- like, it -- to say that there's definitively standing here in this case without any briefing. So I don't know if you can drop a footnote and say this is just a drive-by jurisdictional ruling --

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: -- so you can ignore it in the future. I don't know if you're allowed to do that, but --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: You raised it in the district court.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: We did raise it in the district court. And then we --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But then dropped it before the Sixth Circuit.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: We did. But you know the funny thing about standing arguments, you can't really drop them.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Right.

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: So, if you -- if you're intrigued by that question, you know, I'd be happy to provide supplemental briefing. And -- but I -- but I do think the question really comes down to whether that gobbledegook is sufficiently close to a common law analogue.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Well, this gobbledegook also presents the question of whether it's PII, right, if nobody can look at it and really identify -- only a computer can figure out what this means?

turns.name: PAUL D. CLEMENT
turns.text: Yeah, and maybe that's one more reason to not decide the standing question definitively without more briefing because I do think there is a close relationship between the standing question and the PII question. So, you know, if you say there's standing here because it's sort of not really totally gobbledegook, then my friend's going to try to use that in the lower courts to say, aha, it is personally identifiable information. So, again, I'm -- we're happy to brief it if you'd like us to. But I -- I do think it would be a mistake to definitively decide standing without any briefing.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson? Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Hammack?

turns.name: JOSHUA I. HAMMACK
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Just a couple of points. First, I think it's really important to keep our eye on the ball that what we're looking for here in Section (b)(1) is any consumer of such provider, any consumer. So, when we -- when we have questions about, well, what about someone who purchased a dog bandana or someone who purchased a La-Z-Boy recliner or someone who purchased something or rented something years ago, our question is made simpler by the fact that (b)(1) says any consumer of such provider. So is someone who rented something a number of years ago or purchases a chicken sandwich from a provider, is that person any consumer of such provider? The answer has to be yes. That's the most natural reading. It aligns with ordinary meaning all over the statute. Second, I want to address the -- the point that my friend on the other side made regarding this shift in the number of cases brought happening, you know, a decade or so ago. And that shift did not occur because plaintiffs suddenly woke up one day and discovered the Video Privacy Protection Act. It occurred because of the advent of pixel technology, this technology that all kinds of businesses started embedding in their websites that is automatically target -- tracking and disclosing all sorts of personally identifiable information about you, including the personally identifiable information specifically defined in this statute. Third, that huge liability problem, if we get through all of the various elements of the statute and land in a world where there is large liability, I won't dispute that that's a possibility, but I think it's -- it reflects necessarily the fact that this is a huge scale disclosure regime. That large liability is only possible because of the scope of the disclosures of personally identifiable information here. Fourth, I want to address the mix-or-match point that my friend on the other side made. And I would say it's entirely unsurprising that you might mix or match as between what makes you a consumer and what gives rise to PII. That's exactly why and the direct result of the fact that Congress mentioned two different relationships to two different subject matters from the same source across those two provisions. It's the inevitable consequence of that. To go to Justice Jackson's point regarding the -- the hypothetical that you were discussing with my friend on the other side, I think that exchange really shows the incredible loophole that their reading creates where they can basically structure themselves around VPPA compliance by making sure that you request or obtain video materials or services, but we've structured our business so that you never actually rent, purchase, or subscribe to them. You'll rent, purchase, and subscribe to lots of other things but not those video materials. So, suddenly, we can disclose your personally identifiable information with impunity without your consent. That, I think, should be the anomaly when you're looking at this statute. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
